nodes.label: Alternating Current
nodes.note: AC circuits force steady-state phasor treatment of $R$, $L$, $C$ elements, impedance, resonance, and power factor. JEE Main tests RMS values, LCR resonance, bandwidth $Q$, and transformer ratios. Sinusoidal quantities use $$I(t) = I_0\sin(\omega t + \phi)$$, $\omega = 2\pi f$.

nodes.label: Principles and AC Generation
nodes.note: AC varies sinusoidally; a rotating coil in a magnetic field is the canonical generator. Angular frequency is $$\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi/T$$.

nodes.label: Definition of AC
nodes.note: Alternating current reverses direction periodically: $$I(t) = I_0 \sin(\omega t + \phi)$$ with $\omega = 2\pi f$. One full reversal takes $T = 1/f = 2\pi/\omega$.

nodes.label: Dynamo Principle
nodes.note: A coil of area $A$, $N$ turns, rotating at $\omega$ in field $B$ has flux $NAB\cos\omega t$, so $$\varepsilon = NBA\omega \sin\omega t = \varepsilon_0 \sin\omega t$$. Peak EMF scales with $N, B, A, \omega$.

nodes.label: Average and RMS Values
nodes.note: Average and RMS values connect sinusoidal waveforms to equivalent DC heating effect. RMS of a sine is $$I_{rms} = I_0/\sqrt{2}$$.

nodes.label: Average Value
nodes.note: Over a full half-cycle the mean of $I_0\sin\omega t$ is $$I_{av} = \frac{2 I_0}{\pi}$$. Full-cycle average is zero because positive and negative halves cancel.

nodes.label: RMS Value
nodes.note: RMS is defined by equal heating in a resistor: $$I_{rms} = \frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}, \ V_{rms} = \frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}$$ for pure sinusoids. Mains $230\text{ V}$ means $V_0 \approx 325\text{ V}$.

nodes.label: Form Factor and Hot Wire
nodes.note: Form factor $= I_{rms}/I_{av} = (\pi/2)/\sqrt{2} \approx 1.11$ for a sine wave. Hot-wire instruments read RMS because expansion tracks $I^2R$ heating. Form factor $$= \frac{I_{rms}}{I_{av}} = \frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}} \approx 1.11$$.

nodes.label: Pure Element Response and Phasors
nodes.note: Each pure element responds with a characteristic phase shift between voltage and current. Reactances: $$X_L = \omega L, \ X_C = 1/(\omega C)$$.

nodes.label: Pure Resistor
nodes.note: For $V = V_0\sin\omega t$ across $R$, $$I = \frac{V_0}{R}\sin\omega t$$ in phase with voltage. Average power $P = V_{rms}I_{rms}$ is dissipated as heat.

nodes.label: Pure Inductor
nodes.note: Inductive reactance $X_L = \omega L$ gives $$I = \frac{V_0}{\omega L}\sin\left(\omega t - \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$$ Current lags voltage by $90^\circ$.

nodes.label: Pure Capacitor
nodes.note: Capacitive reactance $X_C = 1/(\omega C)$ gives $$I = \omega C V_0 \sin\left(\omega t + \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$$ Current leads voltage by $90^\circ$.

nodes.label: Phasor Diagrams
nodes.note: Phasors are rotating vectors of amplitude equal to peak value; phase differences come from angles. Adding voltages uses vector sums, e.g. $V = \sqrt{V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2}$. Phasor amplitude equals peak value and angle gives phase lag.

nodes.label: Two-Element Series Circuits
nodes.note: Two-element series circuits combine resistance with reactance in an impedance triangle. Series RL: $$Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (\omega L)^2}$$.

nodes.label: Series RL
nodes.note: Impedance $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (\omega L)^2}$ and phase $\tan\phi = \omega L/R$. Current lags voltage: $$I_{rms} = \frac{V_{rms}}{\sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2}}$$.

nodes.label: Series RC
nodes.note: Impedance $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (1/\omega C)^2}$ and $$\tan\phi = -\frac{1}{\omega C R}$$ Current leads voltage. Used as phase-shift networks.

nodes.label: Series LC
nodes.note: Pure $L$-$C$ has $Z = |X_L - X_C| = |\omega L - 1/\omega C|$, zero at resonance $\omega = 1/\sqrt{LC}$. Voltages across $L$ and $C$ can far exceed the source. Series LC impedance: $$Z = \left|\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C}\right|$$.

nodes.label: Series LCR and Impedance
nodes.note: Series LCR generalizes impedance and phase for arbitrary frequency; operating regimes split by $X_L$ versus $X_C$. Series LCR impedance: $$Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$$.

nodes.label: Impedance Triangle
nodes.note: Total impedance combines resistance and net reactance: $$Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$$ Voltage triangle: $V = \sqrt{V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2}$.

nodes.label: Phase Angle
nodes.note: The phase of current relative to voltage satisfies $$\tan\phi = \frac{X_L - X_C}{R}$$. Inductive above resonance, capacitive below, zero at resonance.

nodes.label: Operating Regimes
nodes.note: If $\omega L > 1/\omega C$ circuit is inductive; if less, capacitive; equality gives unity power factor. JEE graphs ask sign of $\phi$ versus $\omega$. Phase sign of $$\tan\phi = (X_L - X_C)/R$$ tells the circuit character.

nodes.label: Resonance and Quality Factor
nodes.note: At resonance the series LCR current is maximum, phase is zero, and the $Q$ factor measures sharpness. Resonance frequency: $$\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC}$$.

nodes.label: Series Resonance Condition
nodes.note: Resonance occurs when reactances cancel: $$X_L = X_C \Rightarrow \omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}, \ f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$$. Impedance is minimum and purely resistive.

nodes.label: Half-Power Bandwidth
nodes.note: Current falls to $1/\sqrt{2}$ of peak at $\omega_{1,2}$ with $$\Delta \omega = \omega_2 - \omega_1 = \frac{R}{L}$$. Narrower bandwidth means sharper tuning.

nodes.label: Quality Factor
nodes.note: Quality factor is resonance sharpness and voltage magnification: $$Q = \frac{\omega_0 L}{R} = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}} = \frac{\omega_0}{\Delta \omega}$$. $V_L = V_C = QV$ at resonance.

nodes.label: Power and Power Factor
nodes.note: Average power depends on resistive voltage and current alignment; wattless current and chokes matter for efficiency. Average power: $$P = V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos\phi$$.

nodes.label: Average Power
nodes.note: For $V = V_0\sin\omega t$, $I = I_0\sin(\omega t - \phi)$, average power is $$P = V_{rms} I_{rms} \cos\phi = \frac{V_0 I_0}{2}\cos\phi$$ only the resistive part dissipates.

nodes.label: Apparent, Real, Reactive Power
nodes.note: Real power $P = VI\cos\phi$ (watt), reactive $Q = VI\sin\phi$ (VAR), apparent $S = VI$ (VA). Power factor is $\cos\phi = P/S$. Power triangle: $$S^2 = P^2 + Q^2$$ with $S = VI$.

nodes.label: Wattless Current
nodes.note: Current with $\phi = \pi/2$, as in a pure inductor or capacitor, gives zero average power. Energy oscillates between source and element. Wattless current has $$\phi = \pi/2 \Rightarrow \cos\phi = 0$$.

nodes.label: Choke Coil
nodes.note: A choke is a high-inductance coil that drops AC voltage with small $R$, limiting AC current without much heating. Ideal choke has $Z = \omega L$. Ideal choke impedance: $$Z = \omega L$$.

nodes.label: Free LC Oscillations
nodes.note: A lossless LC tank exchanges electric and magnetic energy at its natural frequency. Natural frequency: $$\omega = 1/\sqrt{LC}$$.

nodes.label: Energy Exchange
nodes.note: Total energy sloshes between capacitor and inductor: $$U = \frac{q^2}{2C} + \frac{1}{2}LI^2 = \text{constant}$$ At charge maximum all energy is electric; at $q=0$ all is magnetic.

nodes.label: Natural Frequency
nodes.note: Charge obeys $$\frac{d^2q}{dt^2} + \frac{1}{LC}q = 0, \ \omega = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$$. Adding resistance damps this like a damped oscillator.

nodes.label: Electromechanical Analogy
nodes.note: $L$ plays the role of mass, $1/C$ of spring constant, $R$ of damping: $$m\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} + b\frac{dx}{dt} + kx = 0 \leftrightarrow L\frac{d^2q}{dt^2} + R\frac{dq}{dt} + \frac{q}{C} = 0$$.

nodes.label: Transformers
nodes.note: Transformers step voltage using mutual induction while conserving power up to efficiency losses. Turns ratio: $$\frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p}$$.

nodes.label: Construction and Principle
nodes.note: Primary and secondary coils share flux in an iron core; the turns ratio sets $$\frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p} = \frac{I_p}{I_s}$$ (ideal). Step-up raises voltage, lowers current.

nodes.label: Step-Up and Step-Down
nodes.note: Step-up: $N_s > N_p$, used for transmission at high voltage and low current to cut $I^2R$ loss. Step-down: $N_s < N_p$, used near consumers. Ideal transformer conserves power: $$V_p I_p = V_s I_s$$.

nodes.label: Power Conservation and Efficiency
nodes.note: Ideal: $V_p I_p = V_s I_s$. Real efficiency $$\eta = \frac{V_s I_s \cos\phi_s}{V_p I_p \cos\phi_p} \times 100\%$$ Losses drop as load rises toward rated value.

nodes.label: Energy Losses
nodes.note: Copper loss $I^2R$ in windings, eddy currents in the core (reduced by laminations), hysteresis (soft iron core), and flux leakage between coils. Copper loss scales as $$P_{loss} = I^2 R$$.

nodes.label: Problem Archetypes and Shortcuts
nodes.note: Traps mix DC and AC readings, resonance switching, and hot-wire instruments. Hot-wire reading: $$I_{rms}^2 = I_{DC}^2 + I_0^2/2$$.

nodes.label: DC and AC on Hot Wire
nodes.note: A hot-wire meter reads RMS of the total waveform: $$I_{rms}^2 = I_{DC}^2 + \frac{I_0^2}{2}$$. Superpose mean-square values, not amplitudes.

nodes.label: Voltmeter Across Series LCR
nodes.note: Ideal voltmeters read RMS node voltages. Across $L$ and $C$ at resonance, $V_L = V_C = QV$ while the source reads only $V_R$. At resonance $$V_L = V_C = QV_{source}$$.

nodes.label: Q and Parallel Resonance
nodes.note: High $Q$ circuits respond sharply. Parallel resonance gives maximum impedance and minimum line current, dual to the series case. Quality factor: $$Q = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}$$.

nodes.label: Waveform Parameters
nodes.note: For $I = I_0\sin(\omega t + \phi)$, peak value is $I_0$, frequency $f = \omega/2\pi$, and time period $T = 1/f$. Phase constant $\phi$ shifts the wave along the time axis. Sinusoidal quantities use $$I(t) = I_0\sin(\omega t + \phi)$$, $\omega = 2\pi f$.

nodes.label: Average over Half Cycle
nodes.note: The mean of a sine over its positive half-cycle is $$I_{av} = \frac{2I_0}{\pi}$$. This is why rectified average meters need correction factors for different waveforms.

nodes.label: Hot-Wire Instrument
nodes.note: A hot wire heats as $I^2R$, so its expansion responds to the mean square. Its reading is therefore the RMS value $$I_{rms} = \sqrt{\langle I^2 \rangle}$$ regardless of waveform shape.

nodes.label: Reactance Trends
nodes.note: Inductive reactance $$X_L = \omega L$$ grows with frequency; capacitive reactance $$X_C = 1/(\omega C)$$ falls. At DC an inductor acts like a wire and a capacitor like an open circuit.

nodes.label: Energy Transfer View
nodes.note: At the series LC resonance the inductor and capacitor exchange energy each cycle with no net draw from the source. Source current is limited only by resistance $R$. Sinusoidal quantities use $$I(t) = I_0\sin(\omega t + \phi)$$, $\omega = 2\pi f$.

nodes.label: Power Factor Correction
nodes.note: Industrial loads are inductive, so a capacitor in parallel supplies the reactive part $$Q_C = V^2 \omega C$$. This raises $\cos\phi$ toward unity and cuts line current.

nodes.label: Why High-Voltage Transmission
nodes.note: For the same power, raising voltage by $k$ cuts current by $k$, so line loss $$P_{loss} = I^2R$$ drops by $k^2$. Transformers make this practical.
